blocks.h2: What to Do if Sewage Is Backing Up

steps.body: Every flush, shower and load of laundry adds to the backup. Tell everyone in the house.
Sewage carries bacteria. Don't wade through it, and keep kids and pets out of the basement.
If water is near outlets, appliances or the panel, don't touch them.
Our line is open 24/7. Tell us where the water is coming up and whether it's raining.

blocks.h2: Why Sewage Backs Up in Arlington Heights Homes
blocks.intro: Most backups come down to one of these:

tiles.body: The most common cause in postwar homes. Roots fill the line until water has nowhere to go.
In heavy rain, sewers fill fast. In the combined sewer area near the center of town, they carry storm water too, and it can push back up your floor drain.
A collapsed section or low spot stops flow and catches everything that comes down the line.
Even a healthy line clogs when wipes and grease build up together.

blocks.h2: Sewer Backups and Arlington Heights Basements
blocks.intro: Storm backups are a known problem in Arlington Heights. In July 2011, almost 7 inches of rain fell in just over three hours, on sewers designed for about 2.5 to 3 inches over a full day.

items.body: Homes built before the late 1970s or early 1980s weren't required to have overhead sewers, so many still have basement drains that rely on gravity. When the sewer fills, water finds the lowest opening, which is the floor drain.
Areas like Westgate and Park Manor were hit in 2011. If you've been through a backup before, prevention is worth planning now.
A clean line, a backflow valve and an [overhead sewer system](/arlington-heights/overhead-sewer-systems) each solve part of the problem. We'll tell you which your home needs.

blocks.h2: Sewer Backup Questions From Arlington Heights Homeowners

items.q: Why does sewage come up through my floor drain?
items.preview: It's the lowest drain in the house, so a blockage or overloaded sewer shows up there first.
items.answer: The floor drain is usually the lowest opening in your plumbing. When the main line is blocked or the sewer is full, water rises to the lowest point first. That's why it's often the first sign of a backup.

items.q: Is a sewer backup during a storm my fault?
items.preview: Not always. Your line may be fine and the sewer overloaded. A camera shows which.
items.answer: Not always. If your line is clear, an overloaded public sewer can still push water back into your basement. If roots or a break slowed your line, that's on the private side. We clear it, camera it and tell you which it was.

items.q: Can I clean up a sewer backup myself?
items.preview: Small, contained spills, carefully. Large ones need a cleanup company.
items.answer: A small, contained spill on a concrete floor can be cleaned with gloves, boots and disinfectant. Large backups, or any that reach carpet, drywall or furniture, need a professional cleanup company. Our job is to fix the plumbing that caused it.

items.q: How do I keep it from happening again?
items.preview: Keep the line clear, then add protection like a backflow valve or overhead sewer.
items.answer: Start with a clean, inspected line and regular [sewer maintenance](/arlington-heights/sewer-maintenance). If storms are the trigger, a backflow valve or an [overhead sewer system](/arlington-heights/overhead-sewer-systems) keeps sewer water out.

items.q: My neighbors flooded too. Is it the village sewer?
items.preview: If several homes back up in the same storm, the public sewer was likely overloaded.
items.answer: If several homes on your block backed up during the same storm, the public sewer was likely full. Your own line can still be partly blocked too, so a camera check is worth it before you plan protection.
